findings.text: Participants described a gap between the intended convenience of the single-window/online mechanism and actual experience: physical visits to individual departments reportedly remain necessary even where the application is available online, reducing the practical benefit of the single-window arrangement.

Applicants lack clarity on the sequence of activities, the next requirement, or how the subsequent stage will be communicated; participants associated this complexity with greater dependence on intermediaries.

A common policy approach is applied across sectors with materially different activities (e.g. builders vs. manufacturers), which participants felt does not adequately reflect sector-specific characteristics and requirements.
The discussion points to scope for examining whether CTE requirements can be differentiated more appropriately by sector or activity, where justified.

The principal procedural concern is the disconnect between online availability and the actual applicant journey: applicants continue to interact physically with multiple departments, and information on subsequent steps is not consistently available upfront.
Participants reported limited access to query support outside office hours; Gujarat was cited as a comparison where users could reportedly contact support beyond normal office hours.

No specific instance of duplicate or repeatedly submitted documents was recorded; the burden identified instead relates to multiple departmental interactions and physical visits rather than document duplication.

Participants reported an average delay of approximately 2 to 3 months in obtaining CTE, associated with process complexity, limited visibility of subsequent steps, and the need to coordinate with multiple departments.
Provide a single, comprehensive online source containing the complete CTE process, sequence of steps, requirements, responsible authorities and subsequent stages.
Establish a clear single point of contact (SPOC) for applicants seeking information or clarification on the service.
Make the end-to-end process and subsequent requirements visible to applicants at the outset rather than revealing them progressively.
Strengthen query-support arrangements, including accessible support beyond regular office hours where feasible.
Examine whether CTE requirements can be made more sector-sensitive instead of applying an identical policy approach across materially different sectors.

The regulatory burden experienced by applicants extends beyond formal application requirements: where an online/single-window system still requires multiple physical interactions and applicants discover the process progressively, additional time and coordination costs can arise.
The Gujarat example was raised as a potential reference point for applicant support; participants noted a formal comparison would require verification of the respective service arrangements.

findings.text: Participants reported that obtaining an electricity connection takes 3 to 6 months.
Applicants have to make multiple visits to different departments and offices during the process.
Applicants do not receive clear information on the process and requirements at the outset.
Field visits are not communicated to applicants in advance.
Applicants often do not know which official is responsible for resolving an issue and are directed to another official.
Only one service provider is available in the state, limiting applicants' choice; the number of approved suppliers is also limited, further restricting options.
There is no fixed timeline for completing the electricity connection process.
There is no help desk or single point of contact to guide applicants through the process.
There is no proper grievance redressal system for unresolved issues.
Applicants are not informed in advance about field visits.
The same documents have to be submitted at multiple stages and to different departments, resulting in repeated documentation and additional applicant effort.
Multiple departmental visits, unclear process requirements, the absence of a fixed timeline, and repeated document submission together add to the time required to complete the process.
Difficulty identifying the responsible official and the lack of an effective grievance redressal mechanism can prolong resolution of application-related issues.
Provide a single source of information covering the complete process, requirements, stages and timeline.
Establish a single point of contact (SPOC) or help desk for applicant queries and issue resolution, and clearly identify the official responsible for resolving issues.
Introduce a fixed and clearly communicated timeline for completing the connection process.
Inform applicants in advance about scheduled field visits.
Allow documents already submitted to be reused at subsequent stages instead of requiring repeated submission.
Strengthen the grievance redressal mechanism with a clear escalation channel.
Review the availability of approved suppliers and service-provider options to improve applicant choice.

The overall process places a high coordination burden on applicants due to multiple departmental interactions, repeated documentation, and the absence of a clear point of contact; lack of clear responsibility for issue resolution makes it difficult to navigate the process when problems arise.

Repeated follow-ups required before the field visit is initiated, and lack of advance information about inspection scheduling/rescheduling, add to approval time.

Establish a clear grievance mechanism allowing applicants to report delays and obtain a response without fear of affecting application processing.

Accept 3D-view maps, particularly for high-rise buildings, to make it easier to explain the complete building plan during the Fire NOC process.
The Fire NOC approval process can take 2 to 7 months, resulting in a prolonged approval cycle for establishments.
Users do not have adequate clarity or complete knowledge of the applicable Fire NOC policy and requirements.
Fire safety compliance becomes more difficult when changes suggested by the Fire Department after BPA approval require the building approval process to be taken up again.
The validity of the Fire NOC was suggested to be increased to 5 years instead of requiring renewal at shorter intervals.

Fire NOC requirements should be integrated with the Building Plan Approval (BPA) process, since changes suggested by the Fire Department after BPA approval can require a fresh BPA cycle, creating an additional regulatory cycle.
A system of regular interval-based inspections was suggested as an alternative compliance approach alongside a longer Fire NOC validity period.

Users do not receive sufficient practical guidance from the government on fire-safety requirements for implementation at the establishment level; in the absence of government-led drills, users approach private vendors instead.
Fire-safety guidance (Do's and Don'ts) in regional languages was suggested so business owners can communicate requirements effectively to their employees.

Facilitate regular interaction between the Fire Department and users so regulatory requirements and implementation issues can be discussed directly; conduct regular government-led fire-safety awareness drives and fire drills.
In the absence of government-led fire-safety drills, users currently approach private vendors to arrange fire-safety drills for their establishments.

findings.text: Participants reported a lack of clear information on the renewal process, requirements and next steps, requiring repeated follow-ups to understand what needs to be done.
Even after submitting the application online, users are required to visit the department and submit documents physically, including the same documents multiple times.
Applicants have to make repeated follow-ups after online submission to get the renewal process started; there is no effective application status tracking mechanism.
The inspection process can be delayed when the concerned zonal officer is unavailable; an officer from another zone handling the inspection takes additional time.
There is a significant difference between the 1-year renewal (handled at the zonal office, comparatively easier) and the 5-year renewal (requires approaching the departmental office, more difficult).
Applications handled through intermediaries reportedly receive quicker responses and coordination from the department, making the process appear faster when intermediaries are involved.

The existing grievance redressal mechanism is not effective: escalated grievances are sent back to the lower-level office, requiring the user to coordinate with the same office again. A weekly grievance meeting is held but participants stated users avoid raising complaints for fear of being targeted or facing difficulties in future dealings.
Large-scale industries reportedly receive more regular interaction and handholding from the department than smaller industries.

Unofficial payment demand is identified as a core concern in the factory licence renewal process; users seeking a smoother/faster process often depend on intermediaries to avoid repeated physical visits and follow-up.

Although 1-year and 5-year renewal options are available, participants stated users generally prefer the 1-year option because the 5-year renewal is perceived to involve substantially higher unofficial payments.
Renewal delays can extend to up to one year in some cases.

Participants expressed concern over the high cost and lack of transparency of the Stability Certificate, issued by a recognised competent person under the Odisha Factories Rules, from a limited set of recognised/approved service providers; the rules prescribe competency requirements but not a standard service charge.
Existing licensing slabs/thresholds (e.g. installed power/motor capacity, number of workers) were considered outdated and not reflective of present-day industrial conditions.

Participants highlighted inconsistencies between factory licence and labour-related licence requirements, making it difficult for establishments to reconcile compliance across the two systems; specific areas of mismatch require verification.
The amendment requirement was considered unnecessarily burdensome, particularly where routine changes in manpower, installed power or other factory particulars require a separate amendment process.

Participants stated there is no effective deemed-approval mechanism in practice for delayed renewal cases and suggested applications pending beyond the prescribed period should move forward automatically where conditions are met.

Physical submission of documents is required even after online application, resulting in duplication; participants proposed a common document repository so documents submitted once could be accessed by different departments rather than resubmitted.

Make factory licence renewal genuinely end-to-end online, including document submission; create a central document pool so authorised departments can access documents directly instead of repeated submission.
Handle the 5-year renewal at the zonal office similar to the 1-year process; introduce an effective deemed-renewal/deemed-approval mechanism for eligible pending applications.

Ensure complete transparency in official fees and charges, establish mechanisms to prevent and report unofficial payment demands, and create a transparent/standardised framework for Stability Certificate charges.
Study the practices followed in Telangana and other parts of South India and identify relevant practices that could be adopted to improve the renewal process in Odisha.

findings.text: The Fire NOC renewal process is rigorous and time-consuming, as the complete process has to be followed again at the time of renewal.
Users are required to make physical visits to the department even after submitting the application online.
The limited availability of government-trained Fire Supervisors creates difficulty for establishments in meeting the prescribed requirement.
Renewal delays can extend to up to one year in some cases.
Issues are sometimes raised during renewal even after the Fire NOC was approved earlier, creating inconsistency in the compliance requirements faced by establishments.
During field inspections, penalties are imposed when deficiencies are identified, without adequate time being provided to establishments to rectify the issues.
The current Fire NOC validity is 2 years. Given the rigorous renewal process, the validity was suggested to be increased to 5 years.
Only government-trained Fire Supervisors are permitted and their availability is limited (last known training batches were in 2019 and 2024, with no new batch known since).

The requirement is limited to degree-holder Fire Supervisors (diploma holders and private-trained supervisors not accepted), increasing the financial burden on establishments as degree-holder supervisors command higher salaries.
A deemed approval system was suggested to address cases where the renewal process remains pending for an extended period.

An inspection-based approach was suggested as an alternative to the current renewal system; establishments indicated willingness to undergo regular, including frequent, inspections if Fire NOC validity is extended to 5 years. Maharashtra was cited as an example with no periodic Fire NOC renewal and inspections every six months.
There is no notification or reminder system to inform establishments before the Fire NOC expires.

There is no proper online grievance redressal system; the available complaint box at the department is avoided by users because they fear raising complaints could affect future dealings with the department.
The departmental helpline is inactive after 5:00 PM, limiting access to assistance outside working hours.
Staff shortages affect the availability of officials for field inspections and contribute to delays.
Increase the validity of the Fire NOC from 2 to 5 years; replace the frequent renewal requirement with a longer validity period supported by regular fire-safety inspections.

Introduce a deemed approval system for applications remaining pending beyond the prescribed processing period; introduce advance notifications/reminders before Fire NOC expiry via SMS, email or the portal.

Increase availability of government-trained Fire Supervisors through regular training programmes; allow suitably certified private-sector Fire Supervisors and suitably qualified diploma holders to meet the requirement.
Establish a proper online grievance redressal system with complaint registration, tracking and escalation; extend helpline support beyond 5:00 PM; address staff shortages affecting field inspections.

Provide establishments with reasonable time to rectify deficiencies identified during inspections before imposing penalties, wherever permitted under applicable rules; conduct regular fire-safety awareness drives and fire drills, including for industries employing more than 1,000 workers.

Make the Trade License renewal process fully online and end-to-end, without requiring unnecessary physical visits; improve the stability and reliability of the online portal.

Strengthen monitoring and grievance mechanisms to address reported demands for unofficial payments and ensure applications are processed through a transparent and consistent procedure.

The availability of an online renewal facility does not by itself ensure a user-friendly process; portal reliability, proactive communication and transparent processing are important for the online system to deliver its intended benefit.
The reported experience regarding unofficial payments indicates a need for greater transparency and accountability in application processing.
